steps.title: One open transaction
steps.caption: A forgets to COMMIT: B and C queue for order 497003, then A's next UPDATE closes a cycle.
steps.body: Acme's back-office script runs `UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE id = 497003` in a transaction and then sits **idle in transaction**: nobody has typed COMMIT, so the row lock stays. The warehouse job, which has just updated order 499846, and the shop app both try to update 497003 and wait; at 10 s `pg_stat_activity` shows them 9.0 and 8.0 s into a `Lock` wait, while the support screen's SELECT returned at once. At 20 s the script's next UPDATE asks for order 499846, which the warehouse job holds, and the two transactions now wait for each other.

steps.title: Row locks and the queue
steps.caption: The row lock is xmax in the row: B waits on A's xid, C on the tuple lock, and readers don't wait.
steps.body: An UPDATE that leaves key columns alone takes a FOR NO KEY UPDATE row lock, and PostgreSQL records it in the row itself: the version of 497003 at ctid (774,54) gets `xmax = 165763`, A's transaction ID, so row locks need no shared memory and mostly don't appear in `pg_locks`. The first waiter takes the `tuple` lock on (774,54) and waits for a `ShareLock` on transaction 165763, granted only when A ends; later writers queue for the tuple lock, and readers take no row lock at all. `pg_blocking_pids()` gives the wait-for graph: C waits for B, B for A and A for B, a cycle.

steps.title: Detect, abort, prevent
steps.caption: After deadlock_timeout (1 s) A is aborted with 40P01; sorted locks, timeouts and SKIP LOCKED help.
steps.body: PostgreSQL doesn't look for deadlocks when a wait starts: after `deadlock_timeout` (1 s by default) the waiting process searches the wait-for graph, finds the cycle and usually aborts its own transaction, so A gets `ERROR: deadlock detected` (SQLSTATE 40P01) and B and C finish after 20.0 and 19.0 s. In more runs, locking both orders in id order with `ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` left B waiting 5.5 s without a cycle, `lock_timeout = '2s'` stopped C after 2.0 s (55P03), and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` ended the forgotten transaction. For a job queue, `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` gives each packer a different paid order, and `NOWAIT` fails at once instead of waiting.

steps.title: Schema changes and InnoDB
steps.caption: A waiting ALTER TABLE queues every read behind it; InnoDB detects deadlocks at once and locks gaps.
steps.body: `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN gift_note text` needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, so it waited 7.0 s behind a report's open transaction, and every plain SELECT that arrived meanwhile queued behind the ALTER (6.0 and 5.0 s), although the report blocks no reader. With `SET lock_timeout = '2s'` the ALTER gave up after 2.0 s, reads waited at most 1.0 s, and the retry took 2.6 ms. On MySQL 8.4, InnoDB rolled back A 5 ms after the same cycle formed (`innodb_deadlock_detect` is on by default), and under REPEATABLE READ its next-key and gap locks made new orders for customers 1049 and 1050 wait 3.5 and 4.0 s, where PostgreSQL inserted both at once.
